mortgage-buydown.summary: A temporary mortgage buydown uses subsidy funds to cover part of the early principal-and-interest payments. A 2-1 plan illustrates two years of reduced borrower payments; a 3-2-1 plan illustrates three. The mortgage note rate and lender payment remain unchanged.
mortgage-buydown.scope: Fixed-rate, monthly amortizing loans only. Tax, insurance, mortgage insurance and closing charges are excluded. No eligibility, approval, source-of-funds limits or unused subsidy refund is determined.

examples.title: A 2-1 buydown starts a $300,000 loan at $1,610.46 a month
examples.inputs: $300,000 loan; 7% fixed note rate; 360 monthly payments; 2-1 temporary buydown.
steps: Calculate the lender payment at the 7% note rate over the full 360-month term.
Calculate the first-year borrower payment using 5% over that same original principal and term. The second-year borrower calculation uses 6%.
Subsidy funds cover the difference between the borrower payment and the unchanged contract payment. Taxes and insurance are outside these amounts.
examples.answer: First-year borrower principal and interest is $1,610.46 per month. Budget for the payment increase when each temporary reduction ends.

examples.title: A 3-2-1 buydown spreads the temporary reductions over three years
examples.inputs: The same $300,000, 7%, 360-month loan; select the 3-2-1 plan.
steps: Use borrower calculation rates of 4%, 5% and 6% in years one, two and three, respectively.
For each reduced year, use the original loan amount and original term; the lender continues receiving the 7% contract payment.
Compare total subsidy funding as well as the first-year payment. A lower initial payment can require a larger subsidy.
examples.answer: First-year borrower principal and interest is $1,432.25 per month. The 7% note rate has not changed.

examples.title: A 1-0 buydown provides one year of reduced borrower payments
examples.inputs: $300,000 loan; 7% note rate; 360 months; 1-0 temporary buydown.
steps: Calculate the first-year borrower payment using a 6% calculation rate on the original amount and term.
From year two, the borrower pays the full contract principal and interest. The subsidy is temporary rather than a permanent rate reduction.
examples.answer: The first-year borrower payment is $1,798.65 a month, before taxes and insurance.

examples.title: A 1-1 buydown keeps the same reduction for two years
steps: Use a 6% borrower calculation rate in both of the first two years.
Compare this with the 1-0 example: the first-year payment matches, but the second subsidy year increases total required funding.
examples.answer: The borrower pays $1,798.65 a month in each reduced year. Equal starting payments do not imply equal buydown costs.

questions.question: Does a 2-1 buydown reduce my loan balance faster?
questions.answer: Not in this model. Borrower money plus subsidy makes the same full lender payment, so the balance follows the original note-rate amortization.

questions.question: Does the subsidy include property tax and insurance?
questions.answer: No. The tool calculates principal and interest only. Add escrow and other housing expenses separately.

questions.question: Can I compare 1-0 and 1-1 buydowns here?
questions.answer: Yes. Use the plan tabs; each uses the same original principal, fixed note rate and amortization term.

questions.question: Is total subsidy the same as interest saved?
questions.answer: No. It is funding used to cover part of the borrower’s payments. Contractual interest continues at the unchanged note rate.

sources.title: Fannie Mae: Temporary interest rate buydowns

cash-secured-put.summary: A cash-secured put earns at most the net option premium in this expiration worksheet, while a falling stock can create a much larger loss. Enter a strike, premium, fees and share count, then compare the same position at different expiration prices. The examples below hold those trade inputs constant so the price effect is visible.
cash-secured-put.scope: Manual, standard share-delivery puts held to expiration. No live option chain, fair-value pricing, early-close model, assignment probability or tax calculation. Broker collateral rules can differ.

examples.title: Above the $50 strike: keep $496 net premium
examples.inputs: Strike $50; premium $2.50 per share; two contracts of 100 shares each; $4 total fees; assumed expiration stock price $55.00.
steps: Two contracts × 100 shares cover 200 shares. Gross premium is $2.50 × 200 = $500; subtract $4 total fees to obtain $496 net premium.
At a $55 expiration share price, max($50 − $55, 0) is zero, so there is no intrinsic-value obligation in this scenario.
The $10,000 strike-based cash amount remains a separate collateral measure. The premium does not capture the stock’s upside above the strike.
examples.answer: Modeled expiration profit is $496, the maximum for these trade inputs. Exercise or assignment outcomes are not guaranteed by an assumed price.

examples.title: At $47.52 per share: the position breaks even after fees
examples.inputs: Strike $50; premium $2.50 per share; two contracts of 100 shares each; $4 total fees; assumed expiration stock price $47.52.
steps: Use the same $496 net premium and 200 covered shares.
Breakeven = $50 strike − $496 / 200 = $47.52 per share.
The $2.48 intrinsic loss per share totals $496, offsetting the net premium. Break-even does not mean assignment cannot occur.
examples.answer: Modeled expiration profit or loss is $0, before taxes and any costs omitted from the entered fees.

examples.title: At $45 per share: premium offsets part of a $1,000 obligation
examples.inputs: Strike $50; premium $2.50 per share; two contracts of 100 shares each; $4 total fees; assumed expiration stock price $45.00.
steps: The same trade still receives $496 net premium; do not subtract the $4 fees a second time.
Intrinsic obligation is ($50 − $45) × 200 = $1,000. Subtract it from net premium.
If the shares are delivered at the strike, $47.52 is the modeled net economic acquisition cost per share under these inputs, not a completed tax-basis record.
examples.answer: Modeled expiration loss is $504. A positive premium receipt does not ensure a profitable trade.

examples.title: At a zero stock price: the modeled maximum loss is $9,504
examples.inputs: Strike $50; premium $2.50 per share; two contracts of 100 shares each; $4 total fees; assumed expiration stock price $0.00.
steps: The maximum strike-based share purchase amount is $50 × 200 = $10,000.
At a zero share price, subtract the $496 net premium from that full amount.
Compare this loss with the $496 maximum gain. The premium-to-cash percentage does not describe the possible downside or an annualized return.
examples.answer: Modeled maximum expiration loss is $9,504. The example illustrates substantial downside despite the cash backing.

questions.question: What is the maximum loss on a cash-secured put?
questions.answer: In this expiration model, strike × total shares minus net premium, assuming the stock goes to zero. Fees reduce net premium and increase that loss.

questions.question: Is secured cash the same as naked-put margin?
questions.answer: No. This worksheet uses the full strike-based share purchase amount before premium credit. Broker margin and buying power are separate.

questions.question: Can a cash-secured put be assigned early?
questions.answer: Yes, an American-style put can be assigned before expiration. This tool calculates expiration payoff only.

questions.question: Does the calculator use live option prices?
questions.answer: No. Enter your own premium and scenario price. No real-time quote or valuation model is provided.

profitability-index.summary: Profitability index expresses future net cash-flow present value per dollar of initial investment. NPV expresses the difference in dollars. Keeping the time-zero outlay separate makes the two measures reconcile and avoids counting the initial investment twice.
profitability-index.scope: One positive initial outlay and manually entered future net flows or a known discounted PV. Periodic flows start at the end of period 1. This is not the alternative ratio of positive inflows to all outflows.

examples.title: A $12,000 present value against a $10,000 outlay gives PI of 1.20
examples.inputs: $10,000 initial investment now; $12,000 present value of future net cash flows, already discounted.
steps: Divide future cash-flow present value by the initial outlay: $12,000 / $10,000.
Subtract the same outlay to reconcile NPV: $12,000 − $10,000 = $2,000. Do not discount the entered present value again.
examples.answer: PI is 1.20: $1.20 of modeled future present value per $1 invested. The $2,000 NPV is a separate dollar measure.

examples.title: Three $4,000 receipts fall slightly short at a 10% discount rate
examples.inputs: $10,000 initial outlay; $4,000 at the end of each of years one, two and three; 10% annual discount rate.
steps: Discount each future receipt separately: $4,000 / 1.10, $4,000 / 1.10² and $4,000 / 1.10³.
Their present values total about $9,947.41. Keep the $10,000 time-zero outlay outside that future-flow list.
Divide the discounted receipts by the outlay. The undiscounted $12,000 total alone cannot determine the result.
examples.answer: PI is about 0.994741 and NPV about −$52.59 under these timing and discount assumptions.

questions.question: What does PI equal to 1 mean?
questions.answer: Under this definition, future PV equals the initial outlay and NPV is zero. That is a model threshold, not a guarantee of a suitable investment.

questions.question: Should I include the initial investment in the future cash-flow list?
questions.answer: No. Enter it once as a positive initial outlay. The list starts with the first future period-end flow.

questions.question: Can a project with lower PI have higher NPV?
questions.answer: Yes. Differently sized projects can have a lower value-per-dollar ratio but create more total modeled dollar value.

questions.question: Can I enter negative later cash flows?
questions.answer: Yes. They stay in the numerator as future net flows. Do not confuse this definition with a ratio that moves every outflow into the denominator.

return-on-equity.summary: Corporate return on equity compares period net income with average book equity. The three-factor DuPont identity separates the same ratio into profitability, asset turnover and leverage. Numerator, denominator and period must describe the same ownership scope.
return-on-equity.scope: Manual corporate accounting ratios. No financial-statement retrieval, equity valuation or property cash-yield model. Nonpositive equity and equity crossings do not receive a healthy performance score.

examples.title: Earn $200,000 on $1.25 million of average equity
examples.inputs: $200,000 period net income; $1,250,000 representative average book equity for the same ownership scope.
steps: Divide net income by average equity: $200,000 / $1,250,000.
Convert the ratio to a percentage. Use book equity, rather than the market value of the company’s shares.
examples.answer: ROE is 16% for the entered period. This is an accounting return, not a shareholder’s market return.

examples.title: Estimate average equity from $1 million and $1.5 million balances
examples.inputs: $200,000 period net income; beginning book equity $1,000,000; ending book equity $1,500,000.
steps: Divide same-period net income by that average. Large within-period changes may require a more representative average.
examples.answer: The two-point average gives 16% ROE. It matches the known-average case because the denominator is the same.

examples.title: Reconcile 16% ROE through margin, turnover and leverage
examples.inputs: $200,000 net income; $2,000,000 sales; $2,500,000 average assets; $1,250,000 average equity.
steps: Asset turnover is $2,000,000 / $2,500,000 = 0.8; the equity multiplier is $2,500,000 / $1,250,000 = 2.
Multiply 10% × 0.8 × 2. The identity explains the same accounting ratio without treating greater leverage as an automatic improvement.
examples.answer: DuPont ROE is 16%, using consistent income, asset and equity definitions.

questions.question: Should I use beginning, ending or average equity?
questions.answer: Use a representative average for the income period. The two-point mode averages beginning and ending balances; it may miss material changes during the period.

questions.question: Can ROE be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. A loss divided by positive average equity gives negative ROE. Nonpositive equity needs a different interpretation and is flagged here.

questions.question: Why is DuPont unavailable when sales are zero?
questions.answer: Net margin divides income by sales. At zero sales that factor is undefined, even if direct income/equity ROE can still be calculated.

questions.question: Is this a real estate return-on-equity calculator?
questions.answer: No. It models corporate net income and average book equity, not property cash flow divided by current sale equity.

sources.title: Harvard Business School Online: Return on equity

72t.summary: A substantially equal periodic payment series may qualify for an exception to the 10% additional tax on early retirement distributions if its requirements are satisfied. Notice 2022-6 describes three calculation methods. The amount alone does not establish or qualify a series.
72t.scope: First-year estimates for a new single-life traditional IRA series starting from 2023 onward under the rules checked here. No joint lives, inherited accounts, pre-2023 transition, first-year proration, tax eligibility, recapture calculation or installment administration.

examples.title: An age-50 RMD-method illustration uses a 36.2-year divisor
examples.inputs: Birth August 15, 1973; series starts December 1, 2023; entered December 31, 2022 valuation of $400,000; Single Life table.
steps: Age in the illustrated first distribution year is 50. The selected Single Life expectancy is 36.2 years.
Divide the entered account balance by 36.2. This is the RMD calculation method for a SEPP illustration, not a regular age-based required distribution.
The calculator does not establish that the valuation choice or distribution arrangement qualifies for an exception.
examples.answer: The illustrated first-year annual amount is $11,049.72. Later-year RMD-method amounts require new inputs and the applicable rules.

examples.title: A 4% fixed-amortization illustration gives a different annual amount
examples.inputs: Same birth, 2023 start date and $400,000 valuation; 4% entered annual rate; both optional prior-month AFR fields left at zero.
steps: Use the 36.2-year Single Life period and the entered 4% rate in the level annual-payment formula.
The zero AFR entries mean no prior-month AFR data were supplied; they are not historical rate observations. Check rate eligibility separately.
This calculator uses a single-life, annual-payment illustration and does not establish SEPP qualification or a compliant payment calendar.
examples.answer: The illustrated annual payment is $21,101.63, before any ordinary income tax. The 4% rate is an example, not a current rate recommendation.

examples.title: Fixed annuitization uses mortality weights rather than a single term
examples.inputs: Same age-50, 2023-start $400,000 illustration; 4% entered rate; optional prior-month AFR fields left at zero.
steps: Use the model’s specified IRS mortality table and year-end-payment convention to calculate a single-life annuity divisor.
Divide the balance by that divisor. Mortality-weighted annuitization and fixed-term amortization need not produce the same payment.
Confirm eligibility, permitted rates, account segregation and modification rules separately; this first-year calculation is not a full SEPP plan.
examples.answer: The modeled annual amount is $22,030.33 under the stated mortality and timing convention, before ordinary income tax.

questions.question: Is 72(t) the same as SEPP?
questions.answer: SEPP is a substantially equal periodic payment series associated with an exception under Section 72(t). This page groups the related calculator task and compares three methods.

questions.question: Does the RMD method mean I already owe an age-based RMD?
questions.answer: No. SEPP can use an RMD calculation method before the age for ordinary owner RMD obligations. The tasks and applicable rules differ.

questions.question: Can I choose any interest rate below the entered ceiling?
questions.answer: The tool permits a nonnegative selected rate up to the stated ceiling. Verify the relevant IRS monthly figures and all series requirements separately.

questions.question: Does switching from a fixed method to RMD end the five-year obligation?
questions.answer: No. A permitted one-time switch does not remove the original continuing-period requirements.

questions.question: Are the payments automatically tax-free?
questions.answer: No. An exception may address the 10% additional tax; ordinary income tax and other requirements can still apply. The tool does not determine eligibility.
